items.question:
A strategy consultant at a boutique advisory firm includes the instruction "cite only sources published after 2022" in a competitive analysis prompt. The output includes a 2018 McKinsey study on digital transformation and a 2019 Bain report, both cited as if they meet the recency requirement.

What is the MOST likely explanation?

options.A: Claude misread "after 2022" as "after 2019" due to an internal date parsing error.
options.B: Upgrade to Opus, which applies date-scoped citation constraints more reliably than other model tiers.
options.C: Claude's citations draw from parametric memory — it cannot filter its training knowledge by date. To enforce recency, supply the post-2022 sources directly in the prompt and instruct Claude to cite only those provided documents.
options.D: Use Research mode so Claude can retrieve genuinely recent sources that satisfy the date constraint automatically.

items.question:
A guest relations manager at a luxury hotel chain asks Claude to draft an apology letter to a long-stay guest whose bill was incorrectly charged for three nights. The draft is accurate and professional but uses formal legal phrasing: "Pursuant to your notification, we acknowledge the aforementioned discrepancy and will effect a correction thereto."

What single change BEST resolves the register mismatch?

options.A: Provide a more detailed account of the billing error so Claude can write with more specificity and empathy.
options.B: Reduce the prompt length to give Claude fewer procedural details to mirror in the output.
options.C: Switch to Sonnet, which defaults to a warmer, more customer-facing register for hospitality content.
options.D: Specify the brand voice and audience context: "Warm, personal, luxury hospitality tone addressed to a valued long-stay guest; avoid legal language, use conversational sentences."

items.question:
A quality engineer at a tier-1 automotive manufacturer is using Claude to help complete 8D problem-solving reports. When the engineer asks for a thorough response, each 8D section runs to 400–600 words. When the engineer asks for brevity, the sections collapse to single sentences that fail to meet the process requirements. The standard requires 80–120 words per section with full factual coverage.

Which TWO changes are MOST likely to produce consistently on-specification 8D sections? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Use chain-of-thought prompting to make Claude reason through each step before writing the section.
options.B: Specify the exact word range per section: "Write each section in 80–120 words. Include all required factual elements; do not pad with repetition."
options.C: Provide a completed example 8D section at the target length, showing the expected density and factual coverage.
options.D: Switch to Opus, which produces outputs calibrated to professional quality standards without explicit length guidance.
options.E: Ask Claude to write the section and then count the words, requesting a revision if the count is outside the range.

items.question:
A clinical trial coordinator at a contract research organisation asks Claude to help draft a protocol deviation report for a minor procedural deviation that occurred during a Phase II trial. The report is internal regulatory documentation. Claude declines, citing concerns that generating clinical content could affect patient safety.

What is the MOST accurate diagnosis of why the refusal occurred, and the BEST targeted fix?

options.A: Claude lacks context that this is professional regulatory documentation drafted by a trained CRO professional for institutional review, not clinical advice to a patient. Adding this context — role, documentation type, review chain — repositions the task and addresses the safety concern.
options.B: Switch to Opus, which has broader clinical research content permissions than other model tiers.
options.C: Rewrite the prompt to avoid clinical terminology; Claude's content policy restricts outputs that use technical medical language.
options.D: Build a Project with CRO protocols and trial documentation templates so Claude understands the professional environment before engaging with clinical tasks.

items.question:
An editorial planner at a digital media company provides Claude with 10 draft article topics and asks: "Which of these topics will perform best for Q4?" Claude responds with a quality assessment of the writing in each topic brief rather than a performance ranking.

What is the PRIMARY problem, and what fix is MOST directly targeted at it?

options.A: Provide Claude with historical traffic and engagement data from previous Q4 content cycles to enable genuine performance prediction.
options.B: The question was ambiguous — 'perform best' has multiple meanings; restate as 'rank these topics by expected Q4 SEO traffic potential' and include the relevant performance context or criteria.
options.C: Number the article topics sequentially so Claude knows to evaluate each one individually rather than comparing them as a set.
options.D: Ask Claude to explain its assessment of each topic, then manually extract the performance-relevant points.

items.question:
An environmental analyst at a renewable energy developer asks Claude for an analysis of permitting challenges for a 50 MW solar project on agricultural land in a specific rural county. The output is a generic overview of solar permitting challenges applicable to any US project — no county-specific issues, no agricultural land nuances.

What is the BEST immediate fix?

options.A: Upgrade to Opus, which has deeper knowledge of state and county-level solar permitting processes.
options.B: Use Research mode so Claude can retrieve current permitting regulations specific to that county.
options.C: Supply the project-specific details — county name, zoning classification, land type, project scale, and any known local planning constraints — and ask Claude to focus its analysis on those specifics.
options.D: Add a chain-of-thought instruction asking Claude to reason through each permitting challenge before summarising.

items.question:
A demand planner at a consumer goods company uses Claude to perform ABC inventory classification on 500 SKUs. A single SKU frequently lands in category A on one run and category B on the next. The current prompt defines A as "high value," B as "moderate value," and C as "low value" with no numerical thresholds.

What is the MOST effective prompt change to achieve consistent classifications?

options.A: Upgrade to Opus, which applies more consistent judgement on quantitative classification tasks.
options.B: Use the API with a low temperature setting to reduce sampling variability in classification outputs.
options.C: Build a Project with the company's inventory management policy so Claude understands the classification context.
options.D: Replace the adjective-based definitions with explicit numerical thresholds: "A = top 20% of SKUs by annual revenue contribution; B = SKUs ranked 21–50%; C = remaining SKUs."

items.question:
A data engineer at a fintech company uses Claude to extract transaction metadata from a batch of payment records and return it in a specific JSON schema. The output is syntactically valid JSON but is wrapped in markdown code fences and preceded by the sentence: "Here is the extracted transaction data:" This breaks the downstream parser that expects raw JSON only.

Which TWO prompt changes most directly fix this? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Add an explicit instruction: "Return only valid JSON. Do not include any surrounding text, explanation, or markdown formatting."
options.B: Provide the exact target JSON schema as an example in the prompt with a note: "Your output must follow this schema exactly, with no additional text."
options.C: Switch to Opus, which produces raw JSON output without code fences when given a schema.
options.D: Use XML tags to delimit the output section so Claude places the JSON inside the tags and nothing outside them.
options.E: Ask Claude to validate its own JSON before returning it to ensure the output parses correctly.

items.question:
A policy writer at a city government uses Claude to draft policy documents. Every output includes an unrequested section headed "Legal and Regulatory Considerations" with generic advice to consult legal counsel. The prompt makes no mention of legal review. The policy writer has correctly diagnosed the symptom: Claude is adding an unsolicited advisory section to every document.

What should she do NEXT?

options.A: Add a negative constraint to the prompt: "Do not include a legal review section, legal caveats, or recommendations to consult counsel. Limit your output to the policy content requested."
options.B: Build a Project with detailed system instructions for all policy writing tasks so the constraint persists across sessions.
options.C: Remove all legal or regulatory language from the source material before providing it to Claude.
options.D: Switch to Haiku, which is less likely to append advisory caveats to professional document outputs.

items.question:
A communications director at a children's literacy non-profit asks Claude to write an excerpt for the organisation's annual donor impact report. The excerpt is accurate and data-rich but reads like a statistics bulletin — dense with percentages, cohort comparisons, and regression references.

What single prompt addition MOST directly produces an appropriate register for donors?

options.A: Provide more programme outcome data to give Claude richer material to work with in the report.
options.B: Specify the intended audience and tone: "Write for general donors with no research background; use one or two specific child stories to illustrate impact; keep statistics to two or three headline numbers."
options.C: Switch to Sonnet, which produces a more narrative and emotionally resonant writing style than other model tiers.
options.D: Ask Claude to rewrite the section in "plain language suitable for a non-specialist audience."

items.question:
A category manager at a large grocery retailer asks Claude for promotional product recommendations. The prompt includes: "Do not recommend our own private label products." The output includes two private label items labelled as "excellent value options."

What is the MOST reliable prompt change to enforce this exclusion?

options.A: Reposition the instruction to the very end of the prompt, immediately before the request, so it is processed last.
options.B: Break the task into two prompts: first ask Claude to list all relevant products, then ask it to filter out private label items.
options.C: Replace the negative instruction with a positive scope and a negative reinforcement: "Recommend only nationally branded products. Do not include any retailer-owned or private label items. For example, recommend Heinz, not [RetailerName] Ketchup."
options.D: Provide a list of all private label brand names so Claude can recognise and exclude them from recommendations.

items.question:
A partner at a strategy consulting firm asks Claude for insights on a specific client's digital transformation strategy. The 2,000-word prompt includes the client's industry, revenue, the transformation roadmap summary, and 18 months of initiative performance data. The output is polished but generic: "Prioritise quick wins in customer-facing channels," "invest in data infrastructure." A senior associate proposes upgrading to Opus.

What is the MOST likely root cause and BEST fix?

options.A: Upgrade to Opus, which synthesises complex multi-source data into client-specific strategic insights rather than generic recommendations.
options.B: Add chain-of-thought prompting so Claude reasons through the client's specific data before formulating recommendations.
options.C: The prompt provided data but did not instruct Claude to reference it; adding 'Base every recommendation on specific data from the context above; cite at least one figure or initiative name per recommendation' is the targeted fix.
options.D: Shorten the prompt to the most critical data points so Claude focuses rather than averaging across all inputs.

items.question:
A patient education coordinator at a community health centre asks Claude to write plain-language summaries of three common medication side effects for laminated patient handouts. Claude declines, stating it cannot provide medical advice or medication information.

Which TWO actions are MOST likely to resolve the refusal and produce useful handout content? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Switch to Opus, which has broader medical content permissions for healthcare professional use cases.
options.B: Add professional context: "This is for a clinical team at an accredited health centre producing patient education materials reviewed by a supervising pharmacist before distribution."
options.C: Build a Project with the health centre's patient education policy documents so Claude understands the institutional context before generating content.
options.D: Reframe the task as summarisation of provided prescribing information documents rather than generation of medical advice: upload the medication package inserts and ask Claude to simplify the side-effects section for a lay reader.
options.E: Enable Research mode to allow Claude to access verified medical databases for side-effect information.

items.question:
A business analyst at a strategy consultancy asks Claude to write a one-paragraph executive overview of a merger rationale for a board pack. The output is four paragraphs covering strategic fit, financial projections, integration risks, and stakeholder communication.

What single prompt change MOST reliably enforces the single-paragraph requirement?

options.A: State the hard constraint: "Write exactly one paragraph of no more than 80 words covering only the primary strategic rationale."
options.B: Add 'be brief and concise' to the instruction so Claude understands that brevity is required.
options.C: Switch to Haiku, which produces shorter outputs by default and will respect the one-paragraph request more reliably.
options.D: Provide a one-paragraph example executive overview from a prior board pack so Claude matches the length.

items.question:
A medical information officer at a pharmaceutical company pastes a full prescribing information document into Claude and asks: "What adverse events are not mentioned in this prescribing information?" Claude returns a comprehensive list of all adverse events that are mentioned in the document.

What is the PRIMARY cause of the answer mismatch?

options.A: The prescribing information document is too long for Claude to process fully, causing it to summarise what it can access.
options.B: The critical negation ('not mentioned') was the focal point of the question but was not prominent enough; restate explicitly: 'I am specifically asking what common adverse events for this drug class are ABSENT from the document — not what is present in it.'
options.C: Use chain-of-thought prompting to force Claude to reason about what could be missing before summarising what is present.
options.D: Add a list of all known adverse events for the drug class so Claude can compare against the document and identify gaps.

items.question:
A quantitative analyst at a hedge fund asks Claude to extract strategy risk factors from a research memo and return them in a nested JSON structure: a top-level `strategies` array containing objects, each with a `risk_factors` array nested inside. The output is valid JSON, but all risk factors appear in a top-level `risk_factors` array with `strategy_id` fields rather than nested under each strategy object.

What is the MOST effective fix?

options.A: Replace JSON with XML, which represents hierarchical relationships more naturally than flat JSON arrays.
options.B: Ask Claude to fix the nesting in a follow-up message, specifying the relationship between strategies and risk factors.
options.C: Provide the exact target JSON schema with a populated example showing one complete strategy object with its nested risk_factors array, and instruct Claude to follow this schema precisely.
options.D: Switch to Opus, which handles multi-level JSON nesting more reliably than other model tiers.

items.question:
An HSE manager at an oil and gas operator includes this instruction in a prompt for field safety procedure documentation: "Write at a Flesch reading ease score of 70 or above." The output scores 38 when checked, which corresponds to college-level reading difficulty — unsuitable for field workers who need clear, simple instructions.

What is the MOST accurate explanation of what happened?

options.A: Claude's training did not include the Flesch readability formula, so it cannot compute or target a specific score.
options.B: Flesch readability score calculation requires a separate tool and is not a capability Claude can apply to its own output.
options.C: A Flesch score of 70 is unrealistically high for technical safety documentation; Claude defaulted to a score it judged appropriate for the content domain.
options.D: Readability scores are abstract numeric targets that Claude cannot directly optimise to; specify concrete proxies — short sentences, common words, one idea per sentence, no passive voice — that produce high readability without requiring score calculation.

items.question:
A retail banking product manager at a mid-tier bank asks Claude for a positioning statement for a new high-yield savings account targeting first-time savers aged 22–30. The output reads: "Competitive interest rates, an easy-to-use digital experience, and great customer service." The manager needs a differentiated, audience-specific statement.

Which TWO prompt changes are MOST likely to produce a specific, differentiated positioning statement? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Include the specific product features, interest rate, digital onboarding process, and what makes this account different from three named competitors.
options.B: Switch to Opus, which generates more nuanced and differentiated brand positioning language.
options.C: Define the target customer persona: name, life stage, financial concerns, motivations, and barriers to saving.
options.D: Use Research mode to retrieve positioning statements from competitor savings products for benchmarking.
options.E: Ask Claude to produce five alternative positioning statements and select the most differentiated one.

items.question:
A network operations analyst at a telecoms company classifies incoming fault reports into five categories. Many faults could reasonably belong to two categories. Across multiple classification runs with the same prompt, roughly 20% of tickets receive different category assignments. The analyst needs the classification to be reliable enough for weekly SLA reporting.

What is the MOST effective fix for the borderline-case variability?

options.A: Add disambiguation rules to the prompt: 'When a fault matches two categories, assign the category that corresponds to the primary reported symptom, not the probable underlying cause.'
options.B: Upgrade to Opus to improve classification precision on ambiguous technical content.
options.C: Reduce the number of categories from five to three so fewer fault types span category boundaries.
options.D: Build a Project with the NOC's fault classification taxonomy so the categories persist across all classification sessions.

items.question:
A wealth advisor at a private bank needs to write a quarterly review letter to a long-standing ultra-high-net-worth client. The first draft is accurate and professional but reads like a standard retail investor communication — appropriate for a mass-affluent audience, not for a client managing a multi-generational estate. Two options are on the table.

Which is the BEST corrective action?

options.A: Add more detailed portfolio performance data to the prompt so the letter reflects the client's specific holdings and results.
options.B: Add a targeted persona instruction: "Write as a senior private banker addressing a long-standing client managing a substantial multigenerational estate; the tone should be relationship-led, precise, and acknowledge the client's sophistication without being formulaic."
options.C: Switch to Opus, which produces more sophisticated and personalised writing for high-stakes professional relationships.
options.D: Ask Claude to revise the draft with a more formal and sophisticated tone before sending.

items.question:
A senior researcher at a documentary production company is developing a film on a historical atrocity. She asks Claude to help draft questions for expert historian interviews that discuss specific methods of violence used by the perpetrators. Claude declines, citing concern about content involving violence and harm.

What is the BEST corrective action?

options.A: Remove references to specific methods and focus questions on perpetrator motivation and organisational structure instead.
options.B: Switch to Opus, which has broader latitude for serious historical and journalistic research tasks.
options.C: Add explicit professional and contextual framing: 'I am a documentary researcher; these questions are for academic historian interviews for a film focused on historical accountability; the purpose is testimony, documentation, and public education, not content glorifying violence.'
options.D: Use Research mode so Claude can retrieve existing academic literature on the atrocity and base the interview questions on that material.

items.question:
A grants specialist at a research university asks Claude to draft a Specific Aims section for an NIH R01 application. The output is a single 120-word paragraph. Standard Specific Aims sections for R01 applications run 550–650 words and include a structured overview, three aims with rationale, and expected impact statement.

What is the MOST direct fix?

options.A: Ask Claude to continue from where it left off to expand the draft to the full length.
options.B: Switch to Opus, which produces longer and more elaborated scientific content by default.
options.C: Provide more background on the research project so Claude has more material to work with.
options.D: Specify the required length and structure: 'Write 550–650 words. Structure: (1) overview paragraph, (2) Aim 1 with scientific rationale, (3) Aim 2 with scientific rationale, (4) expected impact statement.'

items.question:
A quality manager at an electronics manufacturer pastes a six-month defect database into a prompt and asks: "Which defect type is most strongly correlated with production line 3?" Claude responds with a summary of all defect types across all four production lines.

Which TWO changes are MOST likely to produce a Line 3-specific correlation analysis? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Switch to Opus, which can handle multi-dimensional data correlation analysis and will focus on the specific line without further instruction.
options.B: Make the specific question prominent and unambiguous: restate it at the end of the prompt as 'For Line 3 only: which single defect type appears most frequently relative to output volume?'
options.C: Use chain-of-thought prompting to force Claude to reason through each line before arriving at Line 3.
options.D: Filter the dataset before providing it: include only Line 3 data in the prompt, or explicitly instruct Claude to base its analysis exclusively on Line 3 records.
options.E: Build a Project with the quality management system data so Claude has persistent access to the full defect database.

items.question:
An investment research analyst at a large asset manager includes 12 specific formatting rules at the very start of a 900-word prompt, followed by 750 words of company financial data and analysis context, followed by a single question. The output satisfies only 7 of the 12 formatting rules. All missing rules were in the first section.

What is the MOST likely cause and the BEST fix?

options.A: Instructions placed early in a long prompt are diluted by intervening content; move the most critical formatting rules to immediately before the question, or use XML tags to isolate them from the data block.
options.B: Claude can reliably apply a maximum of 7–8 concurrent formatting instructions; reduce the rule count to fit within this limit.
options.C: The prompt is too long overall; split it into a formatting-only prompt followed by a data analysis prompt.
options.D: Build a Project with the 12 formatting rules as system-level instructions so they persist without competing with the data context in each prompt.

items.question:
An operations research analyst at a 3PL company asks Claude for route optimisation recommendations for the Dallas–Atlanta corridor specifically, including suggestions to reduce dwell time at the interchange in Memphis. The output is a general discussion of fleet management efficiency principles with no mention of the specified corridor or interchange.

What is the PRIMARY cause of the generic output?

options.A: Upgrade to Opus, which has deeper knowledge of specific logistics corridors and interchange performance patterns.
options.B: The prompt described the corridor and interchange in a context paragraph but did not supply the actual operational data — transit times, load factors, dwell time measurements — for Claude to analyse and reference.
options.C: Use Research mode so Claude can access current corridor performance data from logistics databases.
options.D: Build a Project with the company's routing history and performance benchmarks for the Claude to draw from.

items.question:
A policy analyst at a federal agency needs Claude to produce a briefing note in the standard government format: Issue, Background, Analysis, Recommendation — with two to three sentences under each heading. The output is a free-form essay with no section headings and seven paragraphs.

What is the BEST corrective prompt change?

options.A: Switch to Sonnet, which follows government document conventions more reliably than other model tiers.
options.B: Build a Project with government briefing note templates so Claude has the format available for every subsequent request.
options.C: Specify the exact headings and expected content under each: 'Structure your response using these four headings only: Issue, Background, Analysis, Recommendation. Under each heading, write 2–3 sentences.'
options.D: Ask Claude to reorganise its essay output into the required sections by posting a follow-up message.

items.question:
A clinical data manager at a CRO is using Claude to draft protocol amendment documents. The output structure and content are correct, but every statement is hedged with phrases like 'this could possibly indicate' and 'it might be considered appropriate to.' Protocol amendments require declarative, authoritative language. She has revised the prompt to add an example paragraph from a previously approved amendment — written in the required declarative style.

What should she do NEXT?

options.A: Also switch to Opus before running the revised prompt, to ensure the highest-quality first attempt.
options.B: Also add a persona instruction identifying the author as a senior medical writer before running the revised prompt.
options.C: Also remove the hedging example sentences from the prompt, since showing Claude the problematic language might reinforce it.
options.D: Run the revised prompt and evaluate whether the example is sufficient to shift the register before adding further changes.

items.question:
A proposal manager at a large IT services company is writing a bid response to a UK central government tender for a digital public services platform. The evaluation criteria explicitly require plain English and a non-promotional register. The draft comes back in corporate marketing language — passive constructions, superlatives, and outcome vagueness. TWO fixes are under consideration.

Which TWO are MOST likely to produce a compliant plain-English bid register? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Include register guidance with concrete examples drawn directly from the tender document's own plain-English language: 'Match the register used in the specification — e.g., direct statements like "The system will allow users to" rather than "Our innovative solution enables seamless delivery."'
options.B: Switch to Opus, which avoids corporate marketing language by default on government procurement content.
options.C: Add a persona: 'Write as a public sector delivery professional explaining directly to a procurement evaluation panel how the proposed solution works and what it will deliver — not as a salesperson.'
options.D: Shorten the prompt and remove the commercial background material to reduce marketing-register influence on the output.
options.E: Use Research mode to retrieve examples of successful government bid responses for register benchmarking.

items.question:
A paralegal at a global law firm asks Claude to draft a cease-and-desist letter template for intellectual property infringement cases, to be used as a starting point for attorneys. Claude responds that it is unable to provide legal documents and recommends consulting a licensed attorney.

What is the BEST single change to the prompt to resolve this?

options.A: Add professional context and use framing: 'I am a trained legal professional at a law firm. Draft this as a starting template for internal attorney review and customisation before any client use.'
options.B: Ask Claude what parts of a cease-and-desist letter it can describe in general terms, then assemble the template from those parts.
options.C: Switch to Opus, which has broader permissions for legal document generation tasks in professional contexts.
options.D: Request a 'general overview of cease-and-desist letter components' rather than asking for a draft template directly.

items.question:
A market research analyst at a strategy consultancy asks Claude to identify the top three themes from 30 client interview transcripts. Using the same prompt, run one yields themes named 'Digital friction,' 'Trust deficit,' and 'Value clarity.' Run two yields 'Technology barriers,' 'Brand credibility,' and 'Value proposition.' The underlying content appears to be the same analysis, just labelled differently each time.

What is the MOST effective way to produce consistent theme labelling?

options.A: Switch to Opus, which produces more consistent thematic labelling on qualitative research tasks.
options.B: Provide a defined list of theme names and ask Claude to classify the interview content against that list, rather than generating theme names.
options.C: Process one transcript at a time, naming themes from each individually before aggregating.
options.D: Use a lower temperature setting in the API to reduce label variability across runs.

items.question:
A credit analyst at a community bank asks Claude to draft a credit memo for a $200,000 small business loan. The output is a 2,100-word narrative with extensive industry background, market commentary, and management biographies. The bank's credit policy requires a maximum 400-word memo with four defined sections.

What single prompt instruction most reliably produces a 400-word, four-section compliant memo?

options.A: Ask Claude to summarise its output after writing it, to produce a condensed version of the full memo.
options.B: Switch to Haiku, which produces shorter analytical outputs and is better suited to concise credit documentation.
options.C: Specify the structure and word budget per section: 'Write a credit memo of no more than 400 words total. Sections: Borrower Summary (75 words), Financial Analysis (150 words), Risk Assessment (100 words), Recommendation (75 words). Cover only these sections; omit industry background and management biography.'
options.D: Provide a one-page example credit memo from the bank's historical files so Claude matches the length and format.

items.question:
A bid writer at a professional services firm pastes an 800-word RFP into a prompt containing 15 evaluation criteria across three sections. The final line of the prompt reads: "Address the above." The output addresses 11 criteria and skips four — all of which are in the RFP's third section.

What is the MOST accurate diagnosis and BEST fix?

options.A: Switch to Opus, which can maintain coverage across 15 evaluation criteria more comprehensively than other model tiers.
options.B: Build a Project with the client's RFP so Claude has access to all criteria across sessions.
options.C: Break the response into 15 separate prompts, one per criterion, to ensure complete coverage.
options.D: Replace the vague task instruction with an explicit coverage requirement: 'Respond to each of the 15 evaluation criteria listed above, in order. Address every criterion; do not skip any. Label each response with the criterion number.'

items.question:
An actuarial analyst at a reinsurance company asks Claude to draft a catastrophe risk narrative for a property catastrophe treaty submission covering Gulf Coast windstorm exposure. The output reads: "The geographic area is subject to significant natural catastrophe exposure. Management and monitoring of this risk is essential for treaty pricing." This applies to any catastrophe treaty.

Which THREE prompt additions are MOST likely to produce a submission-specific narrative? (Choose THREE)

options.A: Include the catastrophe model output — modelled loss estimates, return period data, and average annual loss figures for this specific portfolio.
options.B: Reference the specific geographic exposure concentration — county-level or CRESTA zone data, total insured value distribution, and proximity to coastline metrics.
options.C: Specify the structure required by the cedant's treaty template: which sections require loss estimates vs. qualitative narrative vs. risk management description.
options.D: Switch to Opus, which has deeper actuarial knowledge and can generate submission-quality catastrophe narrative without specific model outputs.
options.E: Use Research mode to retrieve current Gulf Coast hurricane loss estimates from public catastrophe model vendors.

items.question:
A content operations lead at an e-commerce company asks Claude to write product titles and instructs: "Write each title in Title Case." Several titles in the batch return in sentence case — for example, "Blue running shoes for men" instead of "Blue Running Shoes for Men."

What single prompt change MOST reliably enforces Title Case across the full batch?

options.A: Add a concrete example alongside the rule: 'Write each title in Title Case. For example: "Blue Running Shoes for Men" not "Blue running shoes for men."'
options.B: Move the Title Case instruction to the end of the prompt so it is the last rule Claude reads before generating.
options.C: Switch to Sonnet, which applies formatting rules more consistently than Haiku across batch tasks.
options.D: Build a Project with content formatting standards so Title Case applies to all future product content tasks.

items.question:
A clinical documentation specialist at a hospital asks Claude to produce a SOAP note — a standard clinical format with sections: S (Subjective), O (Objective), A (Assessment), P (Plan). The output uses the headings History, Findings, Diagnosis, and Treatment Plan instead.

What is the MOST direct fix?

options.A: Switch to Sonnet, which defaults to SOAP format for clinical documentation tasks.
options.B: Specify the exact required heading names and describe expected content: 'Use exactly these four headings: S: (patient-reported symptoms), O: (clinician observations and vitals), A: (clinical assessment and diagnosis), P: (treatment and follow-up plan).'
options.C: Ask Claude to reorganise its output into the SOAP structure in a follow-up message.
options.D: Build a Project with SOAP note templates and clinical documentation standards.

items.question:
An academic journal editor at a research university asks Claude to draft a 150-word abstract for a social science paper on urban food insecurity. The prompt says 'write an abstract.' The output is accessible and well-written — but it reads like a compelling blog post for a general audience, not a peer-reviewed journal abstract.

What is the MOST precise diagnosis of the failure?

options.A: Upgrade to Opus, which defaults to academic register for scholarly content and can produce peer-review-appropriate abstracts without register guidance.
options.B: Provide the full paper text so Claude can match the abstract's register to the existing scholarly language in the paper.
options.C: The prompt omitted the publication context and specialist audience; 'write an abstract' defaults to a general-audience summary. Adding 'for a peer-reviewed social science journal, for specialist academic readers' specifies the register unambiguously.
options.D: Ask Claude to 'use more academic language' in a revision request to shift the register.

items.question:
An anti-money laundering compliance officer at a global bank asks Claude to explain the structural characteristics of shell company networks used in trade-based money laundering, for an internal staff training module. Claude declines to engage with money laundering content.

What is the BEST single prompt change to resolve this refusal?

options.A: Ask Claude what general financial crime concepts it can explain, then build the training content from those component parts.
options.B: Switch to Opus, which has broader compliance and financial crime content latitude in professional contexts.
options.C: Remove the phrase 'money laundering' and substitute 'financial crime risk typologies' to reduce the content sensitivity signal.
options.D: Add explicit professional context: 'This is for an internal AML compliance training module developed by the bank's compliance team. The purpose is to enable staff to recognise and report suspicious activity, not to facilitate it.'

items.question:
A brand strategist at an advertising agency asks Claude for a brand positioning platform for a regional grocery chain founded in 1962 that differentiates on locally sourced produce and long-standing community relationships. The output states: "A trusted, community-focused grocery store offering quality products at competitive prices." This could apply to any regional grocer.

Which TWO changes are MOST likely to produce a differentiated, chain-specific positioning platform? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Include specific brand attributes: founding story details, the percentage of produce sourced locally, named community partnerships, and what national chains in the same markets cannot credibly claim.
options.B: Switch to Opus, which produces more nuanced and brand-aware positioning language for marketing tasks.
options.C: Use Research mode to find positioning statements from comparable regional grocery chains for benchmarking.
options.D: Provide two or three examples of brand positioning platforms from reference brands the client admires, to show the expected depth, structure, and differentiation level.
options.E: Ask Claude to generate five alternative positioning platforms and select the most differentiated one.

items.question:
An internal communications manager at a large manufacturing company asks Claude to write a brief all-hands update on a plant equipment upgrade for a weekly internal newsletter. The output is 260 words across four paragraphs covering equipment specifications, project history, contractor selection process, and future maintenance schedule.

What is the MOST targeted single instruction to enforce brevity?

options.A: Specify the hard constraint and required content: 'Write exactly 50 words. Include only: what is changing, when it takes effect, and one positive message for employees. Omit technical specifications and project history.'
options.B: Switch to Haiku, which produces significantly shorter outputs for internal communications tasks.
options.C: Ask Claude to condense the draft to a single paragraph after producing the initial output.
options.D: Use 'be extremely brief' as an instruction to signal that the required length is much shorter than the default.

items.question:
A network design analyst at an e-commerce logistics provider asks Claude: "Given our current 8-DC network, should we add a 9th DC in Denver to improve transit times to the Mountain West?" Claude responds with a thorough analysis of DC network optimisation frameworks, capacity considerations, and general principles for adding distribution nodes. A colleague suggests the analyst needs to supply more DC performance data.

What is the MOST likely root cause of the mismatch?

options.A: The lack of specific DC performance data prevented Claude from making a data-grounded recommendation; provide the current transit time matrix and volume data for the Mountain West.
options.B: The question was framed as an open-ended strategic question rather than a decision request; reframe as 'Based on the data below, give a yes/no recommendation on adding a Denver DC, with the top three supporting reasons.'
options.C: Use chain-of-thought prompting so Claude works through the trade-offs systematically before arriving at a recommendation.
options.D: Upgrade to Opus, which can make specific network design recommendations from open-ended strategic questions without requiring a prescribed output format.

items.question:
A digital marketing manager at an apparel retailer uses Claude to draft paid search ad copy. Every draft runs 20–30% longer than the character limit and includes comparative language about competitor products — which the prompt never requested and which would violate the retailer's advertising policy. She has correctly diagnosed both symptoms: over-length and unsolicited competitor references.

What should she do NEXT?

options.A: Switch to Haiku, which produces shorter ad copy that is less likely to include unsolicited competitive comparisons.
options.B: Build a Project with the brand's advertising policy guidelines so Claude understands the policy constraints for all future campaigns.
options.C: Revise the current prompt to add two explicit constraints: a hard character limit per ad and a negative instruction prohibiting competitor references.
options.D: Ask Claude to explain why it included competitor references before making any changes, to understand the reasoning.

items.question:
An FP&A manager at a SaaS company asks Claude for a financial commentary update and includes the instruction: "Use no more than three bullet points per section." The revenue section of the output contains seven bullet points.

What is the MOST reliable single change to enforce the bullet count constraint?

options.A: Use a shorter overall prompt so the bullet count instruction has less content to compete with.
options.B: Upgrade to Sonnet, which applies formatting constraints more precisely on financial document tasks.
options.C: Ask Claude to recount its bullets and revise if any section exceeds three.
options.D: Move the constraint to immediately before the output instruction and add a concrete example showing a three-bullet section: 'Use exactly three bullets per section — no more. Example: [three-bullet sample].'

items.question:
A regulatory intelligence analyst at a pharmaceutical company uses Claude to extract regulatory precedents from 50 historical briefing documents. Different runs of the same prompt yield different sets of extracted precedents from the same documents. The analyst needs consistent, comprehensive extraction for a regulatory strategy submission.

Which TWO changes are MOST likely to produce consistent, comprehensive precedent extraction? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Switch to Opus, which performs more consistent extraction on complex regulatory document analysis.
options.B: Define the exact criteria for what qualifies as a regulatory precedent: document type, decision outcome, agency, and decision basis that must be present for an item to qualify.
options.C: Reduce the document set to 10 documents to improve per-document extraction consistency.
options.D: Specify a structured output format with required fields for each precedent — agency, year, decision type, relevance to current application — that forces systematic surfacing of all qualifying items.
options.E: Use the API with zero temperature to eliminate all sampling variability from extraction runs.

items.question:
An operations analytics lead at a parcel delivery company asks Claude to return a JSON object structured as: regions containing hubs, each hub containing an array of lanes. The output is valid JSON but collapses to a two-level structure: regions directly containing lanes, with no hub level. Two remedies are proposed.

Which is the MOST reliable fix?

options.A: Provide a minimal worked example JSON showing one region with two hubs, each hub containing two lanes — the exact three-level nesting required.
options.B: Switch to the API and use function calling to enforce the schema at the infrastructure level.
options.C: Add a more detailed prose description of the nesting relationship: 'Each region must contain a hubs array; each hub must contain a lanes array; lanes must not appear directly under regions.'
options.D: Switch to Opus, which handles deep JSON nesting with greater schema fidelity than other model tiers.

items.question:
A school counsellor at a private secondary school asks Claude to help draft curriculum content for a student wellness programme covering warning signs of anxiety and depression in adolescents. Claude declines, citing concern about providing mental health information that could be harmful if misapplied.

What is the BEST single prompt change to resolve this?

options.A: Remove references to specific mental health conditions and focus only on general wellbeing indicators.
options.B: Add professional context and institutional framing: 'I am a trained school counsellor developing a supervised educational curriculum. This content will be reviewed by clinical advisors before delivery to students. The goal is recognising distress and encouraging help-seeking, not providing diagnosis or treatment.'
options.C: Switch to Opus, which has fewer restrictions on educational mental health content for professional use cases.
options.D: Ask Claude to focus on 'positive mental health' and resilience content rather than warning signs specifically.

items.question:
An ESG analyst at an institutional investment firm asks Claude to draft a section of a shareholder engagement letter to a FTSE 100 company's board of directors on climate-related financial risk disclosure. The output is written in the style of a finance blog — clear and engaging but conversational, with colloquialisms and informal hedging.

What single prompt change MOST reliably shifts the output to an institutional investor register?

options.A: Provide climate disclosure data from the company's last annual report so Claude has substantive content to anchor the formal analysis.
options.B: Switch to Opus, which defaults to more formal and analytically precise writing for financial communications.
options.C: Specify the publication context and formal register: 'This is a shareholder engagement letter from an institutional investor to a listed company's board. Use the formal, measured tone appropriate to fiduciary communication with a board of directors.'
options.D: Build a Project with the firm's prior shareholder engagement letters so Claude can match the established register.

items.question:
A network planning engineer at a telecoms operator asks Claude for a site acquisition risk analysis for a new 5G small cell installation on a residential street in a specific urban borough. The output lists generic categories: 'regulatory challenges, community opposition, structural requirements, aesthetic concerns' — with no site-specific detail.

What is the PRIMARY prompt change needed to produce a site-specific risk analysis?

options.A: Switch to Opus, which has deeper knowledge of telecom site acquisition processes and urban planning regulations.
options.B: Use Research mode to retrieve current planning policies and precedent cases for 5G installations in that borough.
options.C: Chain two prompts: first ask Claude to research 5G urban planning regulations, then apply the findings to the site.
options.D: Include the site-specific details in the prompt — borough name, street classification, proximity to residential properties, local authority planning history, and any known resident concerns — and ask Claude to reference each in its analysis.

items.question:
A procurement analyst at a global professional services firm pastes a list of 12 preferred vendors and asks: "Which of these vendors have a SOC 2 Type II certification?" Claude responds with a general explanation of what SOC 2 Type II certification is, its importance for enterprise procurement, and why firms should verify vendor certifications.

Which TWO changes are MOST likely to produce a direct, vendor-specific answer? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Reframe the task explicitly: 'For each vendor in the list below, state whether they have a SOC 2 Type II certification based on the information I have provided. If the information is absent, state "Not provided."'
options.B: Switch to Opus, which can identify vendor certification status from a list without requiring explicit task framing.
options.C: Place the specific question as the final sentence of the prompt, after the vendor list, so it is the dominant task cue at the point of output generation.
options.D: Use Research mode so Claude can look up current SOC 2 Type II certification status for each vendor.
options.E: Add the vendors' certification documentation to the prompt context so Claude can verify status from provided evidence.

items.question:
A data analyst at a logistics firm asks Claude to generate a complete list of 50 KPI definitions for a dashboard refresh. The response ends mid-sentence after the 31st definition, with no closing remark.

What is the MOST likely explanation?

options.A: Claude reached its per-response output length limit before completing the list.
options.B: The prompt did not supply enough context about the dashboard requirements.
options.C: Claude detected that 31 KPIs already exceeded the analyst's practical needs.
options.D: Claude's training data lacks definitions for the remaining 19 KPI types.

items.question:
A grant writer at a non-profit receives a truncated Claude response. She asked for an 8-section funding proposal narrative; Claude covered sections 1–3 and stopped mid-sentence in section 3. The conversation is still open.

What is the BEST immediate action?

options.A: Start a new chat and resubmit the full prompt with a note asking for all 8 sections.
options.B: Send a follow-up in the same conversation asking Claude to continue from the point it stopped.
options.C: Divide the request into 8 separate chats, one per section, to avoid hitting limits.
options.D: Switch to a higher-tier model to obtain a longer single response.
